study.title: Judges 21 - The lamentation for Benjamin and the morally confused solutions of Israel
study.overview: The chapter closes the narrative with a painful irony: Israel cries the near extinction of Benjamin, but tries to repair the disaster through hasty decisions, thoughtless votes and morally compromising exits. The people recognize the loss of a tribe, consult the Lord, seek women for the survivors and, in the end, the narrator concludes that, without king in Israel, each one did what seemed right in their own eyes. The text shows both real compassion and spiritual and ethical disorder.

outline.title: National mourning and cult after war
outline.explanation: Israel recalls the oath made against Benjamin, goes to the house of God, weeps and asks how a tribe of Israel has almost disappeared. Then it offers burnt offerings and peaceful offerings, showing that the crisis is no longer only military, but also spiritual and moral.

outline.title: The search for wives for the survivors and the case of Jabes-Gilead
outline.explanation: The people investigate who did not participate in the assembly in Mispá, discover the absence of Jabesh-Gileade and destroys that city, sparing only four hundred virgins. These girls are given to the surviving Benjaminites, but still are not enough for the number of the remaining men.

outline.title: Plan to complete women and book completion
outline.explanation: Elders seek to preserve Benjamin's inheritance without formally breaking the oath against giving daughters in marriage. They then guide the Benjaminites to take women in Shiloh during the feast of the LORD. The chapter ends with the return of each group to its inheritance and with the final evaluation of the narrator's absence and subjective morality of the period.

study.context: The chapter resumes the consequences of the civil war against Benjamin narrated in the previous chapters. The people meet in Mizpah, then at Bethel, and mention the house of God and offerings to the LORD. Shiloh appears as the place of the annual feast of the LORD, showing a religious life still organized, although marked by ethical confusion. The text itself explains the period with the repeated formula that there was no king in Israel.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter highlights the gravity of the vows made with precipitation, the weight of the collective consequences of sin and the human inability to correct evil only with religious or political strategies. Israel wants to preserve the unity of the covenant and prevent the disappearance of a tribe, but does so by morally tortuous means. The narrative teaches that external devotion, tears and sacrifices are not enough when it lacks obedient wisdom. The final phrase works as a spiritual diagnosis: when there is no just and faithful government, each person tends to become law for himself. The text does not approve of the narrated acts; on the contrary, it exposes how much a people can deviate even while trying to solve a real problem.

scholarViews.insight: Matthew Henry notes that the narrative shows the ruin of Benjamin and then the provision made for the survivors, including from the virgins of Jabesh-Gilead and the daughters of Shiloh; for him, the story ends in a melancholy manner and highlights the danger of hasty vows, for the less weighting there is before making a vow, the more need there is after striving to fulfill it.

Adam Clarke notes that the Israelites began the war with the intention of totally destroying Benjamin, so that if some men escaped, they did not remain women or descent; he also understands the final phrase as a critique of the narrator, not as approval of the reported atrocities.

questions: What differences are there between genuine repentance and just lamenting the consequences of wrong decisions?
How does this chapter show the danger of trying to correct a sin with another sin?
How does the final phrase describe the effect of the absence of just leadership on the moral life of the people?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to avoid hasty promises, to seek God's will before acting and not to use seemingly good ends to justify wrong means. In practice, it is worth examining decisions made in the heat of emotion, asking for wisdom before committing and recognizing that religious zeal without obedience can produce injustice. It also teaches how to value faithful leadership and community responsibility, so that everyone does not live only according to what seems right to him.
study.uncertainty: The text provided brings some unusual forms of translation and possible variant reading, especially in proper names and expressions such as the description of Silo and the taking of women. The commentators' notes are limited to the excerpts provided; therefore, the synthesis does not include historical, geographical or linguistic details that are not supported by the chapter and the data excerpts.
